the relation between blood pressure and outcomes in patients who have undergone coronary artery revascularization.
the relation between blood pressure (BP), coronary revascularization, and the risk of adverse outcomes.
the relation between blood pressure and outcomes for patients with coronary artery diseases who had undergone previous revascularizations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the management of BP might require modification of targets, according to the revascualrization strategy to improve the outcomes of patients with coronary artery disese.
the relation between BP control and outcomes for patients with coronary artery diseases is complex, and that it is influenced by the revascularization history.
the optimal BP to prevent major adverse events is not known and that the relation between BP levels and outcomes may differ according to revascularization strategy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

patients with coronary artery bypass graft surgery and percutaneous coronary interventions have a higher adverse cardiovascular outcome risk compared to patients with previous percutaneous coronary procedures.
patients with hypertension and CAD who had previously undergone PCI only had a lower risk of adverse outcomes than those who had undergone CABG, with and without PCI.
the optimal BP target to prevent major adverse events in previously revascularized coronary artery disease patients might be different from that for nonrevascularized ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relation between blood pressure and adverse cardiovascular events is not linear and that the relation is different depending on the previous revascularization.
the relation between the major adverse outcomes and BP was J-shaped and accentuated in patients with a prior PCI, compared to a CABG.
the relation of BP to outcomes differs according to the type of revasculation.
